content: During both the intensive and continuation phases of tuberculosis (TB) treatment, individuals of all ages diagnosed with drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB) or drug-resistant TB (DR-TB)—including mono-resistant, poly-drug resistant, rifampicin-resistant, multidrug-resistant (MDR-TB), pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR-TB), or extensively drug-resistant (XDR-TB)—can receive treatment in various settings. These include their households, community-based programs, outreach initiatives, public or private healthcare facilities, or specialized TB hospitals. This applies to both HIV-positive and HIV-negative patients with pulmonary TB (PTB) or extrapulmonary TB (EPTB). In addition to first-line, second-line, and third-line anti-TB drugs, treatment regimens may include retreatment protocols, palliative care, monitoring tests to assess treatment response and adverse events, nutritional evaluations, tracing of patients lost to follow-up, antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV-positive individuals, and mobile health (mHealth) interventions. TB prevention involves screening and treatment to prevent both latent and active TB (PTB and EPTB), particularly among children and HIV-positive adults. Preventive measures include symptom screening to rule out active TB, interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) or tuberculin skin tests (TST), and treatment regimens such as six months of isoniazid (6H), lifelong isoniazid (H), three months of once-weekly isoniazid and rifapentine (3HP), or rifapentine alone. ART regimens for HIV-positive patients and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis are also part of TB prevention strategies. Infection control measures in healthcare facilities, laboratories, congregate settings, and households aim to minimize TB transmission risks. Effective infection control includes early and rapid TB diagnosis, appropriate management of TB patients, and administrative controls to reduce diagnostic delays and initiate prompt treatment. Environmental measures such as ventilation systems, ultraviolet (UV) light fixtures, and laboratory biosafety systems, along with personal protective equipment (PPE), are essential for protecting patients, healthcare workers, and laboratory staff. Congregate settings like hospitals, prisons, refugee camps, and schools require coordinated infection control efforts across sectors. In households, educational campaigns promoting behavioral and social changes are critical to reducing exposure. Above-site TB program services at the national level include strategic planning, development or adaptation of TB care guidelines, program reviews, national and regional meetings, surveys, costing guidelines for TB interventions, management and information systems, supervision, procurement and supply chain management, specimen transportation, advocacy, technical assistance, training, laboratory accreditation and quality assurance, and community education campaigns. These activities are supported by ministries of health, national TB programs (NTPs), reference laboratories, government and non-government research institutes, public and private health facilities, regulatory bodies, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and international partners such as the World Health Organization (WHO). Standardized unit costs for TB interventions are defined to facilitate budgeting and modeling. These costs include direct and ancillary expenses for interventions such as vaccination, outpatient visits, diagnostic tests, patient support, and community events. Costs are calculated per recipient, per intervention, or per output, depending on the activity. For example, costs may be associated with diagnostic tests like microscopy, culture, or molecular assays, as well as treatment regimens for DS-TB, MDR-TB, pre-XDR-TB, and XDR-TB. Costs also cover patient support services, including nutritional assessments, follow-up of defaulters, and community-based treatment visits. TB prevention and treatment costs are further broken down by intervention type, population group, and delivery platform. For instance, costs for treating latent TB infection (LTBI) include expenses for screening, diagnostic tests, and treatment regimens such as 3HP or 6H. Infection control costs encompass administrative, environmental, and personal protection measures in healthcare facilities and laboratories, including biosafety equipment, ventilation systems, and PPE. Overall, these comprehensive measures aim to ensure effective TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and infection control while addressing the financial and operational aspects of TB program implementation.
